A strategy is a total function $V\to V$ and is legal for player $i$ exactly when $E(v,\sigma(v))$ holds for every $v$ with $o(v)=i$; its values at the other player's vertices are unrestricted. The predicate called well formed means exactly that every vertex has an outgoing edge and that the priority function is injective. For any total functions $\sigma,\tau:V\to V$ and start $v\in V$, put $f(u)=\sigma(u)$ if $o(u)=0$ and $f(u)=\tau(u)$ otherwise, and $\pi_t=f^t(v)$ for $t\in\mathbb N$, including $\pi_0=v$. If a vertex of $R$ has priority $p$, classically choose one such vertex $z$; otherwise set $z=v$. Let $k$ be the least natural index for which $\pi_k=z$ if such an index exists, and $0$ otherwise, and let $A=\{\pi_j:0\le j<k,\ p<d(\pi_j)\}$. Write $P_{\sigma,\tau}(v)=(p,A,k)$; $A$ is a set, so repetitions are discarded. Selection among multiple recurring vertices of priority $p$ is by classical choice. This construction is defined without a legality or well-formedness assumption; for an actual start in a finite $V$, some recurring vertex exists and the maximum recurring priority is attained, whereas an empty $V$ has no start. A valuation is any triple $(p,A,k)$ with $p,k\in\mathbb N$ and $A\subseteq V$. Define $r(p)=p$ for even $p$ and $r(p)=-p$ for odd $p$, as an integer. For finite sets $A,B$, write $A\triangleleft B$ if there exists $w$ in their symmetric difference such that $d(u)\le d(w)$ for every $u$ in that difference, and either $d(w)$ is even and $w\in B$, or $d(w)$ is odd and $w\in A$; an empty symmetric difference cannot satisfy this relation, and a maximum-priority witness is not required to be unique. For $a=(p,A,k)$ and $b=(q,B,\ell)$, define $a\prec b$ to mean $r(p)<r(q)$, or $p=q$ and $A\triangleleft B$, or $p=q$, $A=B$, and either $p$ is odd with $k<\ell$, or $p$ is even with $\ell<k$; define $a\preceq b$ to mean $a=b$ or $a\prec b$. This minimization is defined separately at each start and does not assume that $\sigma$ is legal.
